power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Kenya's electronic community health information system (eCHIS) moves household and service data from community health promoters' phones into the national health information system.
When reporting quality falls short, the usual response is more training and competency frameworks.
We tested whether user capability and one-off training explain how well the system performs for its users, or whether continuing support and system stability matter more.
We also examined where quality was lost along the reporting chain.

In this convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study in Kisii County, we surveyed 343 eCHIS users in 22 facility catchments, observed five sites against a structured checklist, and interviewed 13 key informants.
Hierarchical ordinal and logistic regression with facility-clustered standard errors modelled user satisfaction and perceived system consistency.
Formal eCHIS training was near universal (94.5%) and was not associated with either outcome.
Adding continuing support (refresher training, mentorship and technical support response time) significantly improved both models.
McFadden's pseudo-R² for consistency rose from 0.06 to 0.16.
Each faster level of technical support response almost doubled the odds of reporting a consistent system (adjusted odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.35-2.58).
Each step up in crash frequency reduced the odds of higher satisfaction (0.60, 0.43-0.84).
Digital comfort remained independently associated with both outcomes.

At the observation sites, form logic secured completeness (all required fields were filled at 5 of 5 sites), but timeliness (2 of 5), consistency over time (1 of 5) and use of reports for decisions (0 of 4) failed, mostly because of synchronisation.
In open-ended responses, 43.4% of respondents raised the cost of data bundles.
Informants described promoters paying for connectivity and reinstalling the failing application themselves.
Reporting quality depended less on what users knew than on the support around them.
Competency frameworks will need matching standards for connectivity financing, support response and synchronisation monitoring.

Community health workers are often the only contact that rural households have with the formal health system, and the records they keep are the main source of information on what happens at that level.
Electronic community health information systems were introduced to replace paper registers with mobile applications.
These applications capture household and service data at the point of care and pass them to national reporting platforms.

Reviews of community-based health information systems in low-and middle-income countries show that digitisation can improve completeness and timeliness through mandatory fields, automated validation and real-time dashboards.
The same reviews show that these gains are fragile, uneven, and dependent on the conditions in which the systems are run. [1] [2] [3] [4] Kenya has moved quickly in this direction.

text.text: Early Kenyan evaluations report better timeliness and accessibility of community data.
They also report barriers that recur across settings: unreliable connectivity, system downtime, thin technical support and training that is short and seldom repeated 6 .

text.text: Similar patterns appear in Ethiopia, where eCHIS was adopted earlier and has been studied more closely 9-12   The dominant policy response to weak data quality has been to treat it as a problem of the workforce.
Training curricula, digital literacy programmes and, increasingly, national competency frameworks are proposed to close the gap.
The evidence for this response is narrower than its popularity suggests.

Training reliably improves knowledge, confidence and digital skills among community health workers 13, 14 However, the interventions that have improved routine data quality in controlled or implementation studies bundled training with supportive supervision, mentorship, feedback and recognition, and none isolated training as the active ingredient 15, 16 .

text.text: Taken together, these perspectives imply that the quality of a community data stream depends on where along the reporting chain it is examined.
At the point of capture, the application's own form logic can enforce completeness regardless of the setting.
Synchronisation, timely arrival, concordance with source records and use for decisions are different.
They depend on a support ecology of connectivity, power, recurrent financing, technical response and continuing learning that the application does not control (Fig 1).

text.text: The application's form logic secures completeness at the point of capture.
Later stages depend on connectivity, power, recurrent financing, technical support and continuing learning, which the application does not control.
Few studies have tested these competing explanations in the same population, and none, to our knowledge, in a Kenyan county using the national eCHIS.
In this study we used survey, observation and interview data from Kisii County to answer four questions.
First, is one-off formal training associated with how well the system performs for its users?
Second, do continuing support and system performance add explanatory value beyond users' own digital capability?
Third, at which stages of the reporting chain is data quality secured or lost?
Fourth, who carries the costs of keeping the system running?
We argue that, in this setting, reporting quality depended less on what users knew than on the support around them, and that competency-centred reforms will not close the gap on their own.
>Materials and methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials and methods</head>

text.text: We conducted a cross-sectional study using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design.
We administered a structured survey, a site observation checklist, and key informant interviews during the same period and integrated them at the interpretation stage 40 .
text.formatted: We administered a structured survey, a site observation checklist, and key informant interviews during the same period and integrated them at the interpretation stage <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">40</ref> .

text.text: Reporting of the quantitative component follows the STROBE guidelines for cross-sectional studies 40.
text.formatted: Reporting of the quantitative component follows the STROBE guidelines for cross-sectional studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">40</ref>.

text.text: Kisii County lies in western Kenya and comprises nine sub-counties.
CHPs deliver community health services from community units, each linked to a public health facility.
Community health assistants (CHAs) supervise CHPs, and sub-county and county community health focal persons coordinate the programme.
CHPs use the eCHIS application on governmentissued smartphones to register households, record services and referrals, and submit routine reports.
These data are synchronised with the national system.
According to county programme records, the eligible workforce totalled 3,047: 2,940 CHPs, 97 CHAs, nine sub-county focal persons and one county focal person.
The sample size was calculated with Cochran's formula for a proportion (95% confidence, 5% precision, p = 0.5) 41 .
text.formatted: The sample size was calculated with Cochran's formula for a proportion (95% confidence, 5% precision, p = 0.5) <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">41</ref> .

text.text: With a finite population correction for 3,047 and a 5% allowance for nonresponse, the target was 359.
The sample was stratified by sub-county and cadre, and respondents were selected by simple random sampling within strata.
Eligible respondents had used eCHIS in their routine work, were available during data collection and gave written informed consent.
Key informants were selected purposively for their supervisory or coordinating roles.
Observation sites were selected purposively to cover five sub-counties and three levels of facility.
The questionnaire contained 27 items.

They covered respondent characteristics; eCHIS training and its frequency; mentorship; digital comfort and prior digital experience; technical support availability and response time; frequency of system crashes; ease of access; device used; perceived system consistency; satisfaction; staff attrition and retention; and data privacy.
Most items had ordered response categories.
Three items allowed multiple or free-text responses: usage challenges, areas needing improvement, and recommendations.
The questionnaire was pretested with 18 CHPs and its wording simplified where items proved hard to understand.

The observation checklist contained 40 yes/no indicators with space for comments, grouped into five domains: support infrastructure, user conditions, competence, system maintenance and quality of reporting.
Three trained observers completed it at five sites (three hospitals, one health centre and one dispensary) between 22 September and 27 October 2025.
The key informant guide covered the same domains.
We administered it to 13 informants: 11 CHAs, one sub-county focal person, and one county focal person.
We recorded responses as structured summaries against each question in a response template.
The survey did not directly measure data quality.
We therefore analysed two outcomes that capture how well the system performed for its users, and we used the observation and interview data to assess data quality along the reporting chain.
The first outcome was satisfaction with eCHIS on a five-point ordinal scale from very dissatisfied to very satisfied.
The second was perceived system consistency, a binary response to whether the system worked consistently.
Respondents who answered "not sure" (n = 30) were excluded from the main analysis of this outcome.
We grouped explanatory variables into four conceptual blocks.
User capability comprised digital comfort (three levels), prior digital experience (yes/no) and more than six years in community health work (yes/no).
One-off training was a single indicator: whether the respondent had ever received formal eCHIS training.

Continuing support comprised refresher training frequency (never, annually, quarterly or monthly), availability of a mentorship programme (yes/no) and technical support response time (no support received, more than two days, within a day or immediately).
System performance comprised crash frequency (never, once, two to three times or more than three times) and ease of access (four levels).
Ordered predictors were entered as linear scores, so each odds ratio refers to a one-level change.
Descriptive statistics are reported as counts and percentages of all 343 respondents, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals.
We examined bivariate associations using Spearman's rank correlation.
Satisfaction was modelled with proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression 42 , consistent with binary logistic regression.
text.formatted: Satisfaction was modelled with proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">42</ref> , consistent with binary logistic regression.

text.text: We entered the four blocks in sequence (capability, then one-off training, then continuing support, then system performance).
We assessed each block's contribution using likelihood-ratio tests, McFadden's pseudo-R², and the Akaike information criterion.
Standard errors were clustered on the 22 health facilities.
Models used complete cases (n = 307 for satisfaction and n = 281 for consistency).
The largest variance inflation factor among predictors was 1.40.
The proportional-odds assumption was examined by fitting separate binary logits at each cut-point.

We ran four sensitivity analyses: restricting the sample to CHPs, recoding "not sure" responses as "no", replacing technical support response time with technical support availability, and dichotomising satisfaction (satisfied or very satisfied versus the rest).
For the consistency model, we report average predicted probabilities across levels of support response time, with all other covariates held at their observed values.
Analyses were run in Python 3.13 with statsmodels 0.15 and SciPy 1.18.
The analysis code is available with the dataset.
Responses to the three multiple-response survey items were coded with a keyword dictionary into ten categories.
Each category's frequency is reported as a share of respondents who answered the item.
Observation indicators were tallied as the number of sites meeting each criterion, and observer comments were retained verbatim.
Key informant summaries were coded deductively against the PRISM technical, organisational and behavioural domains, with codes added inductively where responses did not fit 35, 43 .

text.text: At capture, the application's design largely ensured quality.
All required fields were completed at every site, and observers noted that a form "if not filled [allows] no submission".
No entries were skipped at four of five sites, and entry formats were standardised at four of five.
Further along the chain, quality fell away.
Data were entered within the recommended timeframe at two of five sites and reports submitted by the deadline at two of five.
Observers attributed the failures to "difficulty in synchronization" and "system failure".
At one site where reports arrived on time, this was "by use of own resources".
Records matched patient registers at three of five sites, and data were consistent over time at only one.
Observers recorded duplicated clients, patients who disappeared from the system after failed synchronisation, and discontinued clients who still appeared as active.
At none of the four sites assessed were eCHIS reports used for decisions.
One observer noted that the reports "does not portray the clear picture on the ground". sites meeting each checklist criterion, grouped by stage of the reporting chain.
The use indicator was recorded at four sites.
The support environment observed at the sites matched these breakdowns.
None of the five sites had user manuals or help guides.
None had an uninterrupted power supply or generator.
One had an alternative power source, one had backup devices and one had regular system maintenance.
Two sites had connectivity during use.
Recent training (within six months) was evident at two sites.
At one site, observers noted that training "was done 2 years ago during implementation".

text.text: Poor connectivity was the most frequently reported usage challenge (75.5%), followed by system downtime or slowness (51.0%).
Inadequate training was cited by 18.1%.

In their free-text recommendations, respondents most often asked for data bundles (46.2% of those who answered), stable internet (39.9%), more or refresher training (32.7%), better-quality replacement phones (22.0%) and payment of the county stipend (15.4%).
Across all three items, 43.4% of respondents cited the cost of data bundles, and 47.8% cited either bundles or stipends.
Users also wanted training.
Availability of training was the improvement area selected most often (63.3%), and online tutorials were the preferred format (49.9%).
This preference was for continuing, accessible learning rather than another round of initial instruction.

Table 6 brings the three strands together.
They converged on four points.
One-off training was near universal and did not explain differences in how the system performed.
Continuing support, especially technical response, did.
Completeness was secured at capture, while timeliness, consistency and use failed at the synchronisation stage.
The recurrent costs of connectivity fell on CHPs.
The main divergence concerned accuracy.
Informants credited eCHIS with more accurate capture, while observers found records matching source registers at only three of five sites.
This difference is consistent with the chain model: data entered accurately can still arrive late, duplicated or incomplete once synchronisation fails.

text.text: Nearly all eCHIS users in Kisii County had been trained, were comfortable with digital tools 358 and could use the application.
Nevertheless, they worked with a system most experienced as 359 inconsistent and produced reports that no one at the observed sites used for decisions.
How well 360 the system worked for users was not associated with whether they had been trained.
It was 361 associated with how quickly help arrived when the system failed, how often it crashed and how 362 easily it could be reached.
Observations and interviews located the loss of quality after the point 363 of capture: at synchronisation, which depended on connectivity that CHPs often paid for themselves.
Data quality in this system came less from what users knew than from the support ecology around them.
These findings fit, and sharpen, the international evidence on training.

Reviews and trials show that training builds knowledge and skill but rarely improves routine data quality on its own, and that successful interventions combine training with supervision, mentorship and feedback 13, 15, 16, 45 .
text.formatted: Reviews and trials show that training builds knowledge and skill but rarely improves routine data quality on its own, and that successful interventions combine training with supervision, mentorship and feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">45</ref> .

text.text: In our data, initial formal training reached almost everyone and made no measurable difference.
By contrast, the continuing-support block explained a substantial share of the variation in both outcomes.
Within that block, technical response time carried most of the independent association.
Refresher training and mentorship were positively associated with the outcomes in bivariate analysis, but they were correlated with each other and with technical support.
This pattern suggests that facilities providing one form of continuing support tend to provide the others.
It agrees with Ethiopian accounts that training without follow-up leaves confidence gaps 9, 10 .
text.formatted: It agrees with Ethiopian accounts that training without follow-up leaves confidence gaps <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: It also agrees with Kenyan reports that short trainings are inadequate 6 6 .
text.formatted: It also agrees with Kenyan reports that short trainings are inadequate <ref type="bibr">6 6</ref> .

text.text: Users in our study wanted more training, but they wanted it continuing and accessible, mostly as online tutorials, which a single induction course cannot provide.
Digital comfort remained independently associated with both outcomes, so individual capability is not irrelevant.
However, its effect fell by a third or more once support and system variables were added.
This is consistent with the idea that users who feel competent are partly those who are well supported.
Competency and support are therefore better understood as joint products of the same environment than as rival explanations.
This matters for policy because a competency framework that certifies individual skill will not, by itself, change the conditions in which those skills are used.
The observation data clarify why training and competence are insufficient.
The eCHIS application enforced completeness by design: a form could not be submitted until required fields were filled.
Completeness, the dimension most often reported as improved by digitisation 1, 3 , was therefore secured at every site.
text.formatted: Completeness, the dimension most often reported as improved by digitisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> , was therefore secured at every site.

text.text: The dimensions that depend on infrastructure were not.
Timeliness, concordance with source registers, consistency over time and use all failed at most sites, and observers and informants linked these failures to synchronisation.
The same sequence has been described in Ethiopia, Uganda and South Africa.
There, connectivity and synchronisation failures delayed uploads and produced duplicated or missing records, and integrated data lagged days behind capture [20] [21] [22] 24 .
text.formatted: There, connectivity and synchronisation failures delayed uploads and produced duplicated or missing records, and integrated data lagged days behind capture <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Our findings add that a single headline indicator such as completeness can conceal these failures.
A county's reported completeness may look good while the data that reach supervisors are late, duplicated and not trusted for decisions.
In PRISM terms, the technical determinants of the system set a ceiling on performance that behavioural interventions cannot raise 35,36 35,36 .
text.formatted: In PRISM terms, the technical determinants of the system set a ceiling on performance that behavioural interventions cannot raise <ref type="bibr">35,36 35,36</ref> .

text.text: In design-reality terms, the application assumed a connected, powered and financed environment that frequently did not exist 37, 39.
text.formatted: In design-reality terms, the application assumed a connected, powered and financed environment that frequently did not exist <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">39</ref>.

text.text: The third finding concerns who pays.
Almost half of respondents raised the cost of data bundles or unpaid stipends without being asked about costs.
Informants described CHPs using their own resources to synchronise and repairing the application themselves by reinstalling it.
Kisii is not unusual in this.

Across low-and middle-income countries, programmes typically finance devices and initial training while the recurrent costs of airtime, data, charging and repair shift to workers 28,31,46 28,31,46. 29 In Tanzania, frontline workers have reported spending more on work data than they earned.
text.formatted: Across low-and middle-income countries, programmes typically finance devices and initial training while the recurrent costs of airtime, data, charging and repair shift to workers <ref type="bibr">28,31,46 28,31,46</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">29</ref> In Tanzania, frontline workers have reported spending more on work data than they earned.

text.text: Our data cannot show whether these costs affected retention, although a third of respondents (33.8%) reported staff retention challenges.
They do show that the timeliness of reporting partly depended on whether volunteers could afford to upload.
Elsewhere, cost-shifting and payment delays have been linked to lower motivation and performance, and digital programmes that covered these costs achieved better retention [32] [33] [34] 47 .
text.formatted: Elsewhere, cost-shifting and payment delays have been linked to lower motivation and performance, and digital programmes that covered these costs achieved better retention <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">47</ref> .

text.text: When a public reporting system depends on private spending by its least-paid workers, its data quality inherits the instability of their finances.
These findings have practical implications for Kenya's eCHIS and for similar systems elsewhere.
The first concerns financing. eCHIS connectivity should be treated as a core programme cost, not a personal expense.
Zero-rating or "whitelisting" eCHIS traffic, which informants proposed, is one way to do this, and direct data reimbursement is another.
The second concerns technical support.
Support should operate to defined service standards, including maximum response times, a reachable help desk, routine maintenance and replacement devices.
Response time was the factor most strongly associated with perceived consistency in our data.
The third concerns monitoring.
Synchronisation should be monitored as a data quality indicator in its own right.

Lag between capture and upload, failed synchronisations and duplicate records can be measured from system logs, and these measures would show the failures that completeness indicators conceal 21, 26 .
text.formatted: Lag between capture and upload, failed synchronisations and duplicate records can be measured from system logs, and these measures would show the failures that completeness indicators conceal <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: The fourth concerns training.
It should be reorganised as continuing support, delivered through accessible online materials, refresher sessions and mentorship linked to supervision, rather than as a one-time event 15, 16 .
text.formatted: It should be reorganised as continuing support, delivered through accessible online materials, refresher sessions and mentorship linked to supervision, rather than as a one-time event <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: A national eCHIS competency framework would be strengthened by including these support standards alongside individual competencies.
This study combined a large survey of eCHIS users with direct observation and key informant interviews in a single county.
All estimates were calculated from record-level data with clustered standard errors and several sensitivity analyses.
The study also has limitations of scope.
First, the design was cross-sectional, so the associations cannot establish direction.
For example, dissatisfied users may judge support more harshly.
Second, the survey outcomes reflect how users experienced the system.
They are not audited measures of data quality, and evidence on data quality itself comes from five observation sites and 13 interviews.
Third, the observation sites were identified at sub-county level and selected purposively, so their results describe conditions at those sites and should not be generalised as county-wide prevalence.
Fourth, key informant responses were recorded as structured summaries rather than verbatim transcripts, which limits the depth of the qualitative analysis.
Fifth, each construct was measured with single items, and some multiple-response items offered preset options, which may have shaped the categories respondents chose.
Sixth, the sample was dominated by experienced CHPs, so new users are underrepresented.
Finally, the study covers one county in the second year of implementation.
Future work should link worker surveys to system logs of synchronisation lag and duplication, compare counties with different financing arrangements, and prospectively test support standards.
Training put eCHIS into the hands of almost every community health promoter in Kisii County.
However, it was not what determined whether the system delivered timely, consistent and usable data.
Those outcomes depended on continuing support, system stability and connectivity, much of which CHPs financed themselves.
Efforts to improve community health data quality in Kenya should finance connectivity, responsive technical support, and synchronisation monitoring with the same priority as competency development.
